title: Saving the kiwi

paragraphs.text: In New Zealand in pre-human times, there were millions of that country’s flightless native bird, the kiwi – possibly as many as 12 million. They occupied all lowland and mid-altitude areas of New Zealand. Nowadays there are only about 80,000 kiwi left, and they occupy less than a quarter of the country. The birds would have become extinct decades ago but for their tough, tenacious nature, their powerful legs and claws for weapons, and their resistance, beyond a certain age and weight, to stoat* attacks. For the past century, New Zealanders have freely exploited the bird’s name and unusual shape without much regard for its welfare in the wild. But recently, a people’s movement has been rallying in support of the people’s bird.

Across the North Island of New Zealand, communities have mobilised to save local kiwi populations, or to create new ones. Farmers and other landowners are also joining the cause of kiwi conservation in unprecedented numbers. They are supporting trapping and poisoning programmes against predators such as stoats. Taken as a whole, these efforts are remarkable: the largest nature conservation movement ever seen in New Zealand in support of a threatened species. This movement began in the mid-1990s, grew stronger by 2000, and has been going purposefully and with far-reaching effects ever since. It involves thousands of volunteers, scores of projects and sponsors, and millions of dollars. In most regions, trust organisations† have grown rapidly to head the campaign, with the Department of Conservation (DOC) surprisingly cast in a secondary role, as an adviser and supporter of many of these projects.

In New Zealand’s South Island too, kiwi have survived long enough to welcome the arrival of help in the form of concerned individuals, Forest and Bird Society volunteers, highly motivated trust organisations, and funding grants from an array of business interests and local government. Reports over the past two decades of a sharp decline in kiwi numbers appear to have sparked this private-sector phenomenon. The Bank of New Zealand’s ‘Save the Kiwi Trust’ was an early contributor, with the bank saying it was shocked to learn that the kiwi could soon be gone from the mainland. By the end of 2005, total allocations from the trust to approved kiwi protection projects had topped the $5 million mark.

Protection for kiwi comes in various forms. Predator-free sanctuaries are the top-of-the-line form, and across all New Zealand the DOC manages, with community support, five kiwi sanctuaries established in 2000 to mark the launch of the New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy. Three are in the North Island: at Tongariro, Coromandel and Whangarei. In addition, there is the privately run Karori Wildlife Sanctuary in Wellington, which was fenced in 1999, and protects a growing population of kiwi known as the little spotted. The two DOC kiwi sanctuaries in the South Island, at Haast and Okarito, are desperately trying to save isolated populations of the birds. Seven more sanctuaries are in the process of being created.

Then there are the four or more predator-controlled areas, where the kiwi population is managed with the aim of increasing numbers. This means that measures are taken to control or eliminate predators, assess kiwi populations and provide a better habitat within clearly defined areas. Intensive trapping of the kiwi’s number one enemy, the stoat, at these places is not only giving local kiwi a chance to thrive but is also doing much to restore biodiversity of other flora and fauna. Kiwi are also highly at risk from dogs which run wild, especially in the North Island. DOC has set itself clear goals: a minimum of 500 pairs of North Island kiwi, and a combined minimum of 300 pairs for the two most seriously threatened populations in the South Island. The 500-pair target for managed populations in the North Island assumes a population of about 1,500 kiwi. It is considered to be a robust number in terms of genetic health. Some of the managed areas have been selected to act as nurseries for juvenile kiwi, allowing them to grow to a size where they are not so much at risk from predators.

A third method of intervention to aid the survival of the kiwi is an artificial hatching and chick-rearing programme called Operation Nest Egg. This is a way of boosting selected kiwi populations in the short- to medium-term. In the North Island, a purpose-built facility at Rainbow Springs in Rotorua is achieving an amazing output on behalf of projects across the central North Island, and Auckland Zoo does a comparable job for the Northland region. Scientist John McLennan says there is a role for less intensively managed kiwi ‘farms’ whose juveniles are released when they can re-stock tracts of North Island habitat that have had fewer mammal pests.

In the South Island, kiwi conservation is largely a DOC job. Most kiwi live in wilderness areas a long way from towns. Their habitats are almost exclusively on conservation land. While Haast and Okarito kiwi populations are now rare and endangered, the great spotted kiwi of Nelson, and the Fiordland and Stewart Island tokoeka (brown kiwi) appear to be just holding their own, unassisted.

Sustaining the current momentum in people power and funding is going to be a challenge, no doubt. But as new technology to control stoats and manage kiwi is developed, the job should get easier and less costly. Although the so-called managed areas, including both fenced sanctuaries and intensively trapped areas, cover only two per cent of the present kiwi domain, they represent a springboard for recovery – a lifeline.

subtitle: No country in the world embraces its national bird as comprehensively as New Zealand does the kiwi – to the point where the people themselves have taken its name. Now, however, New Zealanders are having to fight to save their namesake from extinction.
footnotes: * stoat: a small, furry, meat-eating animal
